title: Tandon Group Chairman M.L. Tandon Continues 50-Year Legacy of Global Innovation and Transformation
subtitle: Reflecting on Five Decades from Punch Cards and IBM to Modern Venture Incubation, FreeCharge, and Empowering India's High-Tech Entrepreneurial Ecosystem
portraitCaption: Manohar Lal (M.L.) Tandon, Chairman of Tandon Group, reflects on a career spanning five decades of global high-tech innovation, electronics manufacturing, and startup incubation.
leadQuote: Social innovation isn't just the right thing to do, it's a key marker of success. You are not only the creators of new standards and technologies; you are the creators of new perceptions that change people’s lives for the better. Approach problems with innovation and tenacity, economically and socially. Think different and do well.
paragraphs: The breathtaking growth and change in the technology world over the past 50 years has touched nearly every aspect of business and daily life. In this sea of revolutionary transformation, there are few constants. Yet, Manohar Lal (M.L.) Tandon, chairman of Tandon Group, has been at the heart of the tech industry from the early days of punch cards and floppy discs, and continues to influence today’s dynamic entrepreneurial community.
Throughout a career spanning five decades, M.L. Tandon has transformed the business community in India and around the world through technological advances, as well as social and economic change.

Today, Tandon Group incubates promising startup companies and operates successful businesses in India and North America. The companies Tandon Group fosters solve significant problems in industries such as IT, healthcare, financial services and e-commerce. In this extensive dialogue with Business Innovators Magazine, M.L. Tandon shares his expertise in, and influence on, industry and innovation in India, overcoming common obstacles and lessons learned through his illustrious career.

qaList.question: Tandon Group has a rich history of innovation with a strong influence over the first floppy drives and first generation of IBM personal computers. What inspired you to start Tandon Group and continue to evolve into the startup incubator it is today?
qaList.answer:
I remember the day I left India to pursue my master’s degree in engineering at Purdue. As I climbed the steps to the airplane, my father pulled me aside and said, “Don’t do anything that would give you, me or your country a bad name. The rest of you is free.” It was a liberating moment for me because I knew I had my father’s blessing to think and do differently, as long as I did something for the higher good. This continues to be a guiding principal and driver behind what Tandon Group continues to do today.

In some ways, the evolution to Tandon Group has been a natural one. I began my career at the IBM Development Lab in San Jose as an engineering manager. I returned home in 1967 to take on a key role at IBM India for nine years until IBM was asked to leave because of non-compliance with Indian Equity norms. When IBM was forced to close its plant in India in 1977, I, along with other key ex-IBMers, proposed to take over the plant. IBM accepted the proposal to give us all assets at the cost of 10 cents to a dollar as long as we employed everyone who had been working in the factory. As a result, we created a company called Pentax Engineering to provide products for the local market in India.

I started Tandon Magnetics in 1978 to supply recording heads to Tandon Corporation, which was founded by my brother Sirang Lal Tandon. We manufactured and exported magnetic heads and storage products as IBM’s preferred supplier for floppy disk drives. We followed up the success of Tandon Magnetics with Tandon Motors in the 1990s, which focused on the manufacturing of motion technologies. That put Tandon Group on the global tech stage as a major supplier and partner for multinational companies including IBM, Hitachi and Toshiba.

In the beginning, I focused on improving manufacturing in terms of process, labor, trade and talent. Today, my family is working tirelessly to take Tandon Group to the next level.

qaList.question: Tell us more about how the next generation of Tandons are leaving their mark.
qaList.answer:
My son Sandeep leads Tandon Group as managing director, focusing on identifying talented entrepreneurs and startups for our group to invest in and incubate. He also serves as chairman of Infinx Healthcare, a software provider for patient access and revenue cycle management for healthcare providers in the United States, as well as Syrma Technology, which continues to provide the world-class electronics manufacturing services the Tandon brand has been built upon.

Jaideep serves as joint director for Tandon Group, Infinx and Syrma and is focused on growing Infinx and Syrma in the U.S. and Europe, as well as building our investment portfolio in the U.S.

Sudeep, also a director of Tandon Group, helped FreeCharge more than double its user base and transaction volume, and onboard more than 500,000 merchants. Now, he is leading innovation at Infinx, specifically focused on artificial intelligence and robotic process automation for its patient access and accounts receivable software.

My daughters-in-law, Gauri and Radhika Tandon, launched a popular Indian-inspired fashion jewelry brand called Isharya after noticing a void in the global market for high quality and well-priced statement jewelry. The brand is carried online at Isharya.com, in international stores like Harvey Nichols, and at its own branded retail stores in Mumbai and New Delhi. Radhika also serves as CMO for Tandon Group, helping Infinx and Syrma with branding, marketing and sales enablement. Sandeep, Jaideep, Sudeep, Gauri and Radhika carry on our rich history of solving industry problems. This is the common thread that has allowed our companies to change how people in India do business in the country and around the world, pioneer progressive workplaces in a state-directed economy and create technology that drives global change. It’s why progress, entrepreneurship, innovation and excellence are part of our mission, and why we’re committed to advancing technological and social innovation by helping next-generation startups in India succeed.

qaList.question: What do you feel are the biggest myths about developing tech startups in India?
qaList.answer: The global community does not recognize the level of innovation growing in India today. The entrepreneurial environment here is very dynamic, not just in terms of manufacturing components, but in new companies and ideas that are transforming industry.

qaList.question: How has manufacturing and technology in India changed over the last five decades?
qaList.answer: When I started the Tandon Mumbai plant in 1978, training the workforce was my top priority because I saw first-hand how corporate efficiency and flawless quality put IBM at the top of the global market. That’s what I wanted for Tandon, but in India we have something called “Chalta hai” – meaning “It’s good enough” or “The little things don’t matter.” But I knew that the little things do matter. Whenever I was on the production floor I would tell the workers “Chalta hai, nehi” or “Chalta hai is not okay!” Today, that spirit has spread to make our workforce second to none in the world.

qaList.question: What are some of the little-known pitfalls or common mistakes founders make on the road to developing tech startups in India?
qaList.answer: The most important element for a successful business is having both technological and social innovation at the core of the business. However, when you are seeking to make change there will always be obstacles. They may involve recruiting the best talent, finding adequate funding, marketing efficiently, or training your workforce. That is true anywhere in the world, not just in India.

qaList.question: How can these pitfalls be avoided?
qaList.answer:
Have the courage to step out of a system that no longer serves you or the world and do things in a different way. In the 1970s, dedicated labor in India was hard to find. The men who typically filled entry-level assembly positions would hop from town to town in search of other options. The costs of constantly training new workers added up quickly. So I stopped hiring men. They could find jobs anywhere. Women, on the other hand, were legally prohibited from working at night. Families often didn’t want them to work because of cultural reasons and no jobs were available to them anyway. But I saw these women as an untapped pool of industrial talent so I hired an all-female electronic assembly team. These women delivered a strong work ethic, loyalty and superior manual dexterity for high-precision electronics assembly.

In this case, the pitfall was the lack of a reliable labor pool, and the solution was to find a way to hire women. The goal isn’t always to avoid pitfalls, but to use innovative thinking and a genuine willingness to embrace change so you can find solutions to inevitable challenges.

qaList.question: Can you share an example of how Tandon Group has helped a tech startup overcome obstacles and succeed in India?
qaList.answer:
Under the leadership of my sons, Sandeep, Jaideep and Sudeep, Tandon Group has focused on investing in tech startups and operating successful companies in India since the early 2000s. One of our most successful startup companies is FreeCharge, which was sold to SnapDeal in India’s largest M&A internet deal. Sandeep co-founded FreeCharge with Kunal Shah, who was one of our business process managers at the time, and Sudeep joined the company later to scale it. Together, they helped FreeCharge get its operations off the ground and double its user base by tapping into the increased penetration of smartphones in India. This has enabled the market to leap from a 90-percent cash-based economy to cardless digital payments. Banks and telecommunication companies had struggled to get Indian consumers online. FreeCharge saw, and capitalized on, the opportunity to target a population with more access to mobile phones than access to the Internet. Getting consumers online required a major change in thinking, but FreeCharge had the courage to bring a good idea to market and they have transformed the way Indians pay.

To help FreeCharge find success despite the obstacles inherent in establishing an entirely new method of payment, Tandon Group helped in recruiting retail partners, nurturing relationships with banks and telecommunications companies to build out the payment platform, raising funds, driving sales, and facilitating hiring for key positions in the company. Each of those elements was necessary to overcoming the central obstacle.

qaList.question: What’s the most important question startup founders should ask themselves as they consider developing tech startups in India?
qaList.answer: India has a thriving economy and entrepreneurship is coming of age right now. Indian entrepreneurs are passionate about solving big problems and making significant change. It is an appealing place to launch your start up. But, you would be wise to consider how much you know about the culture, government and regulations. India is now more welcoming to tech startups than ever before, but you may need to find partners to help you navigate government rules and regulations.

qaList.question: Can you share a lesson you learned early on, that still impacts how you do business today?
qaList.answer:
Social innovation isn’t just the right thing to do, it’s a key marker of success. You are not only the creators of new standards and technologies; you are the creators of new perceptions that change people’s lives for the better. Also, you need to respect every individual on your team. No matter who they are, trust in their ability to do what you want them to do. No matter how big or small the job is, every person is important. Empower your team to take ownership of their work and keep your mind, ears and door open to them. Make your ideas big and keep your business small and nimble enough to succeed. Approach problems with innovation and tenacity, economically and socially. Think different and do well.

Tandon Group has offices in San Jose, Mumbai and Singapore. You can learn more at TandonGroup.com.

sourceNote: Originally published in Business Innovators Magazine (2021). Documenting M.L. Tandon's 50-year legacy of global technology manufacturing, venture building, and industrial transformation across India and North America.

title: Manufacturers to the World: EMS Companies Playing a Stellar Role
subtitle: Exclusive Interview with Mr. M.L. Tandon, Head of Celetron India, on Global High-Tech Outsourcing and the Path to a Billion-Dollar EMS Powerhouse
leadQuote: Nokia does not make the cell-phones that we carry around. It is the EMS companies that do the job for the company. EMS can be termed manufacturers to the world.
paragraphs: Not many would, perhaps, be aware of the stellar role that EMS (Electronic Manufacturing Services) companies play in the making of the modern world. These enterprises provide vital high-precision inputs to almost all modern electronic devices that consumers use daily.

Highly technical in nature and usually operating away from the public glare, these companies have been silently making an indelible mark on global supply chains. One such company is Celetron India, founded by pioneering industrialist Manohar Lal Tandon.

Operating from the Santacruz Electronic Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ) in Mumbai, Celetron exports critical PC and electronics components such as switch-mode power supplies, head stack assemblies for hard disk drives, and memory sub-systems, operating with profit margins in the rarefied 12 per cent region.

In an extensive interview with The Hindu Business Line, Mr. M. L. Tandon spoke candidly about the transformation of contract manufacturing, India's competitive standing against China, and Celetron's roadmap to becoming a billion-dollar hardware enterprise.

qaList.question: What role is the EMS industry playing in driving modernisation?
qaList.answer: Today, we are all very familiar with modern gadgets that define urban and modern living, such as the Palm PDA, the Nokia cell-phone, the IBM notebook and the Microsoft Xbox. These are high-technology gadgets and the brands are ubiquitous, but what many people might not know is that these products are manufactured not by the brand-holders themselves, but by a global industry called the EMS industry. EMS can truly be termed 'manufacturers to the world'. Fewer and fewer famous brands actually make what they sell. Previously, technology was not accessible, but with protection laws in place, companies have begun to outsource. Manufacturing for these companies is becoming capital- and labour-intensive.

qaList.question: What are the advantages that EMS companies provide to the manufacturing companies?
qaList.answer: Many critical advantages. These include rapid time to market as product lifecycles shorten, rapid scale to high manufacturing volumes, sharing of core components across product lines, asset deployment flexibility, and leading-edge manufacturing engineering with substantial cost reduction. It also provides a significant reduction in needed capital expenditure and acts as a stabilizing buffer against demand fluctuations in the consumer end-market.

qaList.question: Can you tell us something about the evolution of the EMS industry?
qaList.answer: The EMS industry has evolved from small- and medium-enterprise entrepreneurs, commonly referred to as contract manufacturers, into sophisticated global service providers. Until the 1980s, contract manufacturers limited their scope to a few specific isolated functions, such as manual board stuffing. Over the years, the digital revolution expanded and demands from consumer, telecom, computer, and network companies surged exponentially. As a result, contract manufacturers started receiving complex integrated projects and transitioning to comprehensive, end-to-end turnkey services.

qaList.question: How did the consolidation take place across the global industry?
qaList.answer: The 1990s can be termed as the decade of acquisitions for the EMS sector, as growth through mergers and acquisitions was a strategic route adopted by leading players. Today, consolidation is driven by larger EMS entities acquiring smaller competitors and purchasing original equipment manufacturers' manufacturing plants to establish immediate local production capacity.

qaList.question: Could you tell us something about the global EMS scenario and international competitors?
qaList.answer: Technology thresholds are exceptionally high in companies catering to consumer electronics, communications, industrial electronics, and networking, and are by far the highest in medical electronics, automotive electronics, and avionics. A significant development has been that China has surged ahead because of immense infrastructure availability; it is worth noting that China has over 500 Special Economic Zones today, while India has only four.

qaList.question: What about the Indian scenario and India's potential on the global stage?
qaList.answer: In the EMS sector, India can become the preferred alternative and emerge as a powerful contender in the global market. I firmly believe that Indian companies should equip themselves with cutting-edge technology, become deeply versed in advanced design, drive new product innovation, and master complex manufacturing. We must avoid duplication of products and inculcate rigorous financial discipline. Trust and transparency in operations will breed enduring confidence in outsourcing relationships. If these steps are taken, India has an extraordinary chance of becoming a front-ranking global player in world electronics and IT hardware trade, projected to exceed $1 trillion by 2008.

qaList.question: What are Celetron's immediate expansion plans?
qaList.answer: We are aggressively expanding our capacities to meet surging domestic and international demand. The Indian arm exports precision PC components such as power supply modules, head stacks for disk drives, and memory cards. In addition to our SEEPZ operations, we are in the process of commissioning a state-of-the-art production facility in Pondicherry. Through these coordinated expansions, we are on track to touch revenues of $1 billion across our domestic and export divisions.

sourceNote: Transcribed and curated from original archival print scan of The Hindu Business Line, Tuesday, April 13, 2004.

title: EFY Top 100: Celetronix India Ranks Among Leading Global EMS Providers
subtitle: Electronics For You Annual Industry Rankings Highlights Celetronix India Surpassing ₹1,000 Crore in Manufacturing Turnover
leadQuote: Celetronix India has surged past ₹1,000 Crore in hardware turnover, solidifying its place among the world's leading tier-one electronics manufacturing providers.
paragraphs: In the definitive EFY Top 100 annual survey of India's electronics industry, Celetronix India Pvt. Ltd. (formerly known as Celetron India) was recognized as one of the country's most formidable global electronics manufacturing powerhouses.

Headquartered at Unit No. 9, SEEPZ, Special Economic Zone, Andheri (East), Mumbai, the company operates ISO 9001:2000 certified manufacturing plants across three strategic hubs: SEEPZ in Mumbai, the Madras Export Processing Zone (MEPZ) in Chennai, and Pondicherry.

Celetronix's manufacturing capabilities encompass high-density micro-electronic assemblies, including head stack assemblies for hard disk drives, wiring harnesses, complex sub-assemblies, fibre-optic components, DRAM modules up to 512 MB, audio amplifiers, satellite receiver boards, set-top boxes, RF-based contactless smart cards, and Switch-Mode Power Supplies (SMPS) ranging from 5W to 1,500W.

Financial figures verified by the EFY survey demonstrate sustained double-digit growth: turnover expanded from ₹852.6 crore in 2001–02 to ₹941.3 crore in 2002–03, and crossed the landmark ₹1,000 crore milestone in 2003–04 to reach ₹1,033.2 crore.
sourceNote: Extracted from EFY Top 100 Annual Industry Survey, Electronics For You, November 2004, Page 81.

title: From the Horse's Mouth: Industry Leaders on Global Scale and Cost Advantage
subtitle: Dataquest Feature on Leading Industrial Captains and the Roadmap to $25 Billion in Hardware Exports
leadQuote: At Celetron, we run a capital-intensive business and rank among the country's largest hardware exporters. A bulk of our orders come our way due to the cost advantage that we offer.
paragraphs: In a special investigative issue examining the structural transformation of India's technology ecosystem, Dataquest convened viewpoints from key captains of industry including M. L. Tandon (Chairman, Celetron India), Kiran Karnik (Chairman, NASSCOM), Vinnie Mehta (Executive Director, MAIT), and L. C. Singh (CEO, Nihilent Technologies).

Highlighting the operational dynamics of global electronics manufacturing, Mr. M. L. Tandon articulated how Indian contract manufacturing had achieved global parity by combining rigorous process automation with disciplined labour economics.

The issue also featured historical Dataquest Top 20 rankings tracking the Tandon Group's pioneering manufacturing entities — Advance Technology Devices, Tancom Electronics, and Ultra Tek Devices — which consistently dominated national hardware export rankings throughout the 1980s and 1990s.
sourceNote: Archival excerpt from Dataquest (Volume XX, Issue 23), December 15, 2002, Pages 60–62.

title: Celetron Inc: Your Preferred Manufacturing Partner — Concept to Completion
subtitle: International Corporate Profile Featured in Fortune Magazine Showcasing India's EMS Cleanroom Capabilities to Global OEMs
leadQuote: India has already been discovered for low cost software industry. The next frontier is manufacturing services and we are the pioneer in this field in India.
paragraphs: Published in Fortune Magazine's international edition, this profile presented Celetron to Fortune 500 decision-makers as India's premier Electronic Manufacturing Services partner, capable of delivering end-to-end concept-to-completion solutions for global technology leaders.
The profile highlighted Celetron's specialized expertise in electromechanical precision assembly, networking infrastructure, data storage devices, computing hardware, and wireless equipment.

Key manufacturing capabilities highlighted include cleanroom-based assembly environments, in-house Chip-On-Board (COB), Chip-On-Flex (COF), and Surface Mount Technology (SMT) lines, patented DRAM partial patching technology, and international safety certifications including UL, CSA, TUV, NEMKO, DEMKO, BABT, and MITI (Japan).

With over 350,000 square feet of certified production floor space and a dedicated cleanroom workforce of 6,000 technicians supported by 750 experienced engineers, Celetron established India's capability to deliver high-volume, mission-critical hardware to the world's most demanding customers.
sourceNote: Reproduced from Fortune Magazine International Corporate Showcase, May 14, 2001.

title: Resurgent Tandon Group Heads for Rs 600 Cr: Magneto Resistive Tech to the Rescue
subtitle: Investigation by Bakul Gala on How the Tandon Group Retooled its SEEPZ Lines with Advanced Thin-Film Technology to Drive a Stupendous Multi-Fold Rebound
leadQuote: Group turnover is heading for a new high of ₹600 crore from this year's ₹330 crore. A newly resurgent Tandon Group has learnt its lessons well, reorganising into Celetron to ensure a more even-keeled future.
paragraphs: There is palpable excitement within the Mumbai-based Tandon Group of companies — India's sole manufacturer of precision head stack assemblies used in high-density data storage drives, comprising Advanced Technology Devices, Tancom Electronics, and Cortech Systems.

Group Chairman M. L. Tandon, who has steered his enterprise through fast-moving technological cycles, expressed supreme confidence as audited group turnover surged back toward ₹600 crore from the previous year's ₹330 crore.

In 1997–98, the group had generated over ₹300 crore in revenues, but encountered intense global headwinds in 1998–99 when hard drive manufacturers transitioned en masse to Magneto-Resistive (MR) recording heads, rendering older inductive head designs obsolete almost overnight.

Demonstrating extraordinary engineering agility, the group retooled its cleanrooms and retrained its workforce to produce cutting-edge Magneto-Resistive assemblies. The results were immediate: Advanced Technology Devices (ATD), an ISO 9002 certified unit, saw its revenues rebound from ₹7.1 crore to ₹175.1 crore in 1999–00 — a stupendous 2,400 per cent surge.
Tancom Electronics registered an equally remarkable 922 per cent revenue recovery over the same period, while Cortech Systems contributed ₹17 crore in certified power supply manufacturing.

To present a unified corporate face to Fortune 500 buyers, Chairman M. L. Tandon orchestrated the consolidation of ATD, Tancom, and Cortech under a single corporate identity — Celetron — establishing unified manufacturing standards and unified quality assurance.
sourceNote: Cover story in Express Computer (IT People), December 4, 2000, Pages 1 & 4.

title: Fotofeature: M.L. Tandon — Putting India on the Hardware Export Map
subtitle: Millennium Honours Profile Commemorating Two Decades of Unbroken Hardware Export Leadership
portraitCaption: Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon photographed at his executive desk in Mumbai for Information Systems Computerworld.
leadQuote: As head of the Tandon Group of companies, M.L. Tandon is responsible for putting India on the hardware export map, topping national export rankings and keeping competitors completely out of sight.
paragraphs: In its special millennium opening edition, Information Systems Computerworld published a prestigious 'Fotofeature' recognizing the visionary industrialists who laid the foundations of India's technology economy.

Among the select titans honored was Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon, Chairman of the Tandon Group, acclaimed as the individual single-handedly responsible for placing India on the global hardware manufacturing map.

The profile celebrated the Tandon Group's diversified precision hardware footprint — spanning data storage sub-assemblies, magnetic recording heads, power conversion systems, and micro-computing peripherals — which dominated national export rankings year after year, outperforming domestic competitors by substantial multiples.

Accompanied by an authentic full-color portrait of Mr. Tandon at his executive desk in Mumbai, the feature commended his resilience in guiding the company through international economic recessions and tech transitions while maintaining Indian manufacturing's reputation for uncompromising quality.
sourceNote: Information Systems Computerworld, January 1–15, 2000 (Vol. XIV, Issue 1), Page 35.

title: M.L. Tandon: Powering One in Every Ten Personal Computers Sold Globally
subtitle: Business Today Investigation Reveals How a SEEPZ Hardware Exporter Captured 10% of the Global PC Power Supply Market
leadQuote: In fact, one in every 10 PCs sold in the world today has a Tandon power supply.
paragraphs: The Tandon Group, operating out of the Santa Cruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ) in Bombay, is the third-largest computer hardware manufacturer in India, trailing only domestic giants HCL-HP and Wipro Infotech. With audited exports of ₹201 crore in 1993–94, Tandon is undisputed as the country's single largest hardware exporter.
Tandon's commanding global success has been built around a rigorous, systematic design of its business model to leverage the distinctive advantages offered by manufacturing out of India.

Explains CEO Manohar Lal Tandon: 'The only factor that is massively in India's favour is low labour costs. And we have always manufactured only those products that have very high manual precision inputs.'

A decisive 95 per cent of Tandon's turnover originates from switch-mode power supplies for personal computers and intricate sub-assemblies that go into hard disk drives, which carry labour-added values exceeding 20 per cent. Because labour costs in traditional Asian tech hubs such as Singapore and Taiwan were significantly higher, Tandon demonstrated that high-volume precision assembly could be carried out far more economically in India.

Tandon's international customer list represents the blue-chip pantheon of global computing: supplying certified power units to IBM and Compaq, and precision hard disk sub-assemblies to Seagate, Western Digital, and Conner Peripherals.
In fact, industry audits reveal that one out of every ten personal computers sold on Earth in 1994 incorporated a Tandon power supply.

Addressing the paramount challenge of maintaining world-class defect-free quality across a large workforce, Mr. Tandon credited the group's in-house training academies: 'With many processes handled by semi-skilled workers, quality is entirely dependent on the effectiveness and discipline of our training systems.'
sourceNote: Business Today, July 7–21, 1994, Page 87.

title: Cover Story: Hardware Heavyweight — How Tandon Became India's Largest Exporter
subtitle: Global Magazine Cover Feature on M.L. Tandon and the ₹221-Crore Industrial Machine Supplying the World's Computing Giants
portraitCaption: Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon featured on the cover of Global: The Magazine on International Business (December 1994).
leadQuote: What makes this ₹221-crore infocorp India's third largest hardware manufacturer — and its undisputed largest exporter.
paragraphs: In an extensive seven-page cover story, Global: The Magazine on International Business dissected the operational genius behind the Tandon Group, an enterprise that single-handedly generated nearly half of India's total computer hardware exports.

The cover featured a striking portrait of CEO Manohar Lal Tandon beneath the banner 'Hardware Heavyweight', examining how an engineer who honed his skills at IBM's San Jose development laboratory returned to India to build a precision manufacturing empire out of Mumbai's SEEPZ.

The investigation highlighted the Tandon Group's multi-plant cleanroom infrastructure, operating across multiple standard design factory units in SEEPZ, dedicated to producing voice-coil actuators, magnetic read/write heads, and high-efficiency power supplies for global titans such as IBM, Apple, Compaq, and Hitachi.

The report underscored Mr. Tandon's pioneering social legacy: establishing high-standard working conditions and securing groundbreaking legal exemptions that allowed women to work across evening and night cleanroom shifts, fostering an 85%+ female workforce renowned for micro-precision assembly dexterity.

Through uncompromising quality control, direct ties to Silicon Valley, and an emphasis on value-added exports, Manohar Lal Tandon demonstrated that Indian manufacturing could stand toe-to-toe with the world's most exacting technology standards.
sourceNote: Cover Story in Global: The Magazine on International Business, December 1994 (Cover and Pages 18–24).

title: Eye-to-Eye with the Toughest Customers: How an Ex-IBMer Built India's Export Giant
subtitle: Computer Express Investigation by Venkatesh Hariharan on How M.L. Tandon Built a ₹221-Crore Hardware Exporter and Sold Precision Tech Back to IBM
portraitCaption: Cleanroom technicians at SEEPZ, Mumbai assembling micro-precision magnetic recording heads. Photo by Vinayaka Prabhu.
leadQuote: Compaq had just released a new PC range and Intel's engineers lost no time in opening it up. And one of the first things they saw was Tandon's power supplies inside, along with its 'Made in India' label.
paragraphs: Two years ago, as M. L. Tandon was working at his office at SEEPZ, Bombay, he was surprised by a call from the United States. The caller was a senior procurement director from the semiconductor colossus — Intel. Apparently, Intel was seeking to source power supplies and had identified Tandon's company as a potential tier-one supplier. But Tandon was mystified: he had never advertised his products in the US. So how did Intel discover his company?

The answer illuminates the fiercely competitive American hardware industry: Compaq had just released a flagship personal computer, and Intel's engineers immediately disassembled it for benchmarking. One of the first components they inspected was Tandon's power supply, bearing an unmistakable 'Made in India' label.

For Tandon, an ex-IBMer and Chairman of the ₹221-crore Tandon Group, that call vindicated a bold decision taken 16 years earlier — to return to India and pioneer a hardware export enterprise from scratch at SEEPZ, Mumbai. While other executives pursued comfortable domestic representation, Tandon took the rigorous path of export manufacturing.

Today, the Tandon Group stands as India's largest computer hardware exporter, supplying Fortune 500 tech leaders including IBM, Compaq, Seagate, Western Digital, and Fujitsu. In a sector growing at 45 per cent annually, Tandon dominates, generating 41 per cent of India's total hardware exports.

Tandon's career began at IBM's San Jose development laboratory in Silicon Valley in 1963, after earning an MS in Engineering from Purdue University and an MBA from Santa Clara University. In 1978, he returned to India, founding Tandon Magnetics at SEEPZ to produce floppy drive heads, stepper motors, and switch-mode power supplies (SMPS).

Operating across nine companies with over 350,000 square feet of cleanrooms and 5,500 personnel, the group delivers products with an average value-addition of 40 per cent. 'We deploy the technology and produce in volume,' says Mr. Tandon. 'We are opening doors, creating customers in companies like IBM and Seagate. If Tandon can do it, other Indian companies can do it too.'
sourceNote: Transcribed from Computer Express investigative feature, September 12, 1994.

title: Cover Story: The Tandon Example — Becoming an Elephant Among Asian Tigers in Exports
subtitle: Computers Today Cover Feature Dissects How Manohar Lal Tandon Proved India Can Out-Compete Southeast Asian Hardware Giants
leadQuote: India can become an elephant among Asian tigers in hardware exports. The Tandon Group has demonstrated that high precision and global scale are completely achievable from SEEPZ.
paragraphs: In an exhaustive cover feature, Computers Today presented the 'Tandon Example' as the benchmark blueprint for Indian economic liberalization and high-tech manufacturing.

While Indian industry had traditionally looked up to the Asian Tigers — Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong, and South Korea — for electronic hardware dominance, the Tandon Group proved that Indian manufacturing, anchored by disciplined cleanroom engineering and cost economics, could out-compete established East Asian players.

Led by Manohar Lal Tandon, the group reached ₹201 crore in pure hardware exports in 1993–94, operating advanced sub-assembly lines at SEEPZ Mumbai producing voice coil actuators, magnetic recording heads, and certified computer power supplies for the world's most demanding computer makers.
The feature commended Mr. Tandon's long-term vision of establishing high-density component manufacturing rather than superficial assembly, laying the groundwork for India's electronic self-reliance.
sourceNote: Computers Today Cover Story, July 1994, Pages 24–30.

title: Fastest-Growing Among the Big: Tandon Group Ranks #1 with 145% Growth
subtitle: Computers Today Annual Survey Names Tandon Group the Fastest Expanding Hardware Enterprise in India
leadQuote: Outpacing every major infotech conglomerate in the country, the Tandon Group recorded a blistering 145.4% expansion in audited hardware exports.
paragraphs: Computers Today's 1997 annual survey of the Indian information technology industry awarded the Tandon Group top honours as the 'Fastest-Growing Among the Big', recording an unprecedented 145.4% annual revenue expansion.

Fueled by surging global demand for high-capacity hard disk drive sub-assemblies through its flagship JTS Technology and Tancom Electronics divisions, the group's export turnover vaulted to ₹622 crore.

The publication noted that while other hardware houses struggled with policy bottlenecks and shrinking domestic margins, Mr. M. L. Tandon's unswerving focus on international export processing zones allowed the group to operate with friction-free global efficiency.
sourceNote: Computers Today Annual Industry Rankings, July 1997.

title: Long Term Strategy For Exports Required: Exclusive Interview with M.L. Tandon
subtitle: Comprehensive Policy Dialogue with M.L. Tandon on Labour Reforms, Export Infrastructure, and Strategic Global Competitiveness
leadQuote: In the international market, the customer is supreme. To compete with China and Southeast Asia, India must craft long-term stable export policies that reward speed, quality, and scale.
paragraphs: In this extensive interview with Indian Export Products, Chairman Manohar Lal Tandon laid out a strategic roadmap for the Government of India to position the country as an indispensable global manufacturing destination.

Drawing upon his experience building multi-hundred-crore manufacturing operations at SEEPZ, Mr. Tandon outlined the critical policy interventions required: rationalizing import-export procedures, providing competitive power and telecommunications infrastructure, and updating archaic labor regulations to allow round-the-clock cleanroom shifts.

He highlighted that export manufacturing is fundamentally an issue of uncompromising discipline: delays of even 24 hours at air cargo hubs or customs checkpoints jeopardize international contracts, necessitating world-class logistics for Indian enterprises.
sourceNote: Indian Export Products, November 1996, Pages 12–15.

title: Presidential Address to Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh on Export Zone Policies
subtitle: Historic Address by Mr. M.L. Tandon, President of FEPZAI, Advocating Economic Modernization to Union Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh

metrics.label: Dignitary Present
metrics.value: Hon'ble Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh

metrics.label: Forum
metrics.value: Federation of EPZ Associations in India (FEPZAI)

leadQuote: In the international market, the customer is supreme, whereas we in the zones feel procedures are supreme. Let us dismantle administrative hurdles so Indian industry can compete freely on the world stage.
paragraphs: Delivered before Hon'ble Union Finance Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh in New Delhi, this presidential address by Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon (serving as President of the Federation of Export Processing Zones Associations in India - FEPZAI) remains one of the seminal speeches in modern Indian economic reform.
Mr. Tandon directly presented the ground realities faced by Indian manufacturers attempting to export to Fortune 500 customers in the United States, Japan, and Europe.

He challenged the prevailing bureaucratic mindset: while international clients demand speed, flexibility, and flawless quality, Indian export units were constrained by rigid procedural compliance. His speech catalyzed pivotal reforms in customs clearances, duty drawback rationalization, and bank credit availability for export unitholders across all Indian processing zones.
sourceNote: Official transcript of the Presidential Address delivered at the FEPZAI National Conference, New Delhi, 1994.

title: Rs. 2,370 Crore Consumer Electronics Export Expected: Observations at CETMA Seminar
subtitle: Keynote Address by Mr. M.L. Tandon on Expanding India's Global Market Share in Consumer and Industrial Hardware
leadQuote: India has the technical acumen and disciplined engineering capability to capture a decisive share of the international electronics market.
paragraphs: Speaking before the Consumer Electronics and TV Manufacturers Association (CETMA) seminar, Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon projected that India's electronics hardware exports would exceed ₹2,370 crore by 2001–02 if proper policy alignments were enacted.
He stressed the urgent necessity of moving from low-margin component trading toward high-density precision manufacturing, cleanroom surface mounting, and integrated sub-assembly exports.
His observations served as an industry benchmark, guiding both public sector planners and private manufacturers in building scalable hardware facilities.
sourceNote: CETMA News Annual Convention Proceedings, 1996.

title: Welcome Address by Shri M.L. Tandon, Chairman ESC, to Commerce Minister P. Chidambaram
subtitle: Chairman's Address at the National ESC Export Awards Ceremony in New Delhi with Commerce Minister P. Chidambaram
leadQuote: Indian hardware and software exports have entered a golden era. Our entrepreneurs have proven that Indian products can meet the world's most rigorous benchmarks.
paragraphs: As Chairman of the Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC), sponsored by the Ministry of Commerce, Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon welcomed Hon'ble Union Minister of Commerce Shri P. Chidambaram to the national export awards ceremony in New Delhi.

Mr. Tandon celebrated the collective achievement of Indian exporters in breaking through international trade barriers and highlighted the need for sustained institutional support to ensure Indian electronics companies could expand from sub-components into complete computing and telecommunication systems.
sourceNote: Elsoftex Newsletter, Volume XVI, February 1996, Pages 1–3.

title: Tandon Earns Laurels in Exports: Presidential Award Presented by Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma
subtitle: National Recognition for the ₹240-Crore Tandon Group Conferred at Rashtrapati Bhavan by President of India

metrics.label: Conferred By
metrics.value: President of India Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma

leadQuote: Tandon, a ₹240-crore turnover group accounting for 41% of the country's computer hardware exports, was conferred the National Award for Outstanding Export Performance by the President of India.
paragraphs: The October 1995 edition of Elsoftex Newsletter celebrated the conferment of India's highest national export honor upon the Tandon Group by Hon'ble President of India, Dr. Shankar Dayal Sharma, at Rashtrapati Bhavan.

The citation recognized the Tandon Group's pioneering contribution to precision micro-hardware manufacturing at SEEPZ, Mumbai, noting that the enterprise had maintained undisputed leadership as India's premier foreign exchange earner in the electronics sector.
sourceNote: Elsoftex Newsletter, October 1995, Page 1.

title: Letter of Strategic Commendation from Hitachi Metals Executive Directorate
subtitle: Official Letter from Tokyo Directorate of Hitachi Metals Ltd. Commending Tandon Group's World-Class Quality Standards
leadQuote: Hitachi Metals conveys its utmost respect and appreciation for the exemplary manufacturing quality, engineering precision, and integrity demonstrated by the Tandon Group.
paragraphs: On March 4, 1996, the executive directorate of Hitachi Metals Ltd., headquartered at Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo, transmitted an official letter of strategic commendation honoring the Tandon Group.

The Japanese multinational commended Mr. M. L. Tandon and the group's manufacturing units at SEEPZ for adhering to zero-defect standards in assembling high-density magnetic recording head assemblies, cementing an enduring bilateral technology partnership between India and Japan.
sourceNote: Official diplomatic and corporate transmission from Hitachi Metals Ltd., Tokyo, Japan, March 4, 1996.

title: Discover the Fascinating World of Tandon: Manufacturing 49% of India's Hardware Exports
subtitle: Comprehensive Archival Corporate Monograph Detailing the Group's 9 Cleanroom Plants, Technologies, and Global Client Base
leadQuote: Tandon: India's largest manufacturing exporter of computer systems, switch mode power supplies, magnetic recording heads, and voice coil motors.
paragraphs: This 15-page historical corporate monograph offers an exhaustive chronicle of the Tandon Group's industrial footprint at SEEPZ, Mumbai.

The monograph documents the group's manufacturing ecosystem across nine specialized operating units, detailing the production of Winchester head stack assemblies, sub-micron voice coil actuators, multi-output SMPS power systems, stepper motors, and precision computer peripherals.

It chronicles the company's pioneering social commitment: establishing world-class cleanrooms staffed predominantly by female technicians (comprising over 85% of the cleanroom workforce), supported by in-house training schools, subsidized meals, medical dispensaries, and transportation.

The publication verified that in 1994–95, the Tandon Group single-handedly accounted for 49 per cent of the entire Republic of India's computer hardware exports, establishing a benchmark of industrial excellence that earned praise across the global technology landscape.
sourceNote: Archival Corporate Monograph: 'Discover the Fascinating World of Tandon', Published 1995.

title: Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ): Historical Overview & Growth
subtitle: Comprehensive Economic Survey of SEEPZ Mumbai's First 15 Years and the Pioneering Rise of Magnetic Hardware Manufacturing
byline: R. M. Premkumar, Development Commissioner, SEEPZ
leadQuote: SEEPZ contributed to the extent of more than 66 per cent of total electronics exports from the country, with high-technology magnetic heads and floppy drives leading the vanguard.
paragraphs: Authored by the Development Commissioner of SEEPZ, R. M. Premkumar, this definitive historical study examined the fifteen-year trajectory of the Santacruz Electronics Export Processing Zone in Bombay from its founding in 1974 through 1990.
The survey demonstrated that SEEPZ became the preeminent engine of Indian electronics exports, accounting for up to 66.5% of total national electronics exports during the 1980s.

The report specifically highlighted the emergence of precision computer peripherals — floppy disk drives, Winchester recording heads, and power conversion units pioneered by Manohar Lal Tandon's manufacturing companies — which transformed SEEPZ from a nascent zone into a globally respected hardware hub.
sourceNote: Industrial Electronics & Development (IED), June–July 1990, Pages 1–7.

title: EFY Top 100: Celetron India Surges Past Rs 1,000 Crore in EMS Turnover
subtitle: Electronics For You Annual Rankings Highlights Celetron India Crossing ₹1,000 Crore Milestone in Hardware Exports
leadQuote: Celetron India has entered the rarefied four-figure turnover club, surpassing ₹1,000 Crore in pure electronic manufacturing exports.
paragraphs: In the December 2002 issue of Electronics For You, the annual industry rankings spotlighted Celetron India as one of only a handful of electronic manufacturing enterprises to breach ₹1,000 crore in turnover.

Operating out of Mumbai's SEEPZ zone alongside sister plants in Chennai (MEPZ) and Pondicherry, the company consolidated its leadership as India's primary export supplier of sub-micron head stack assemblies, DRAM memory units, and power conversion electronics to global PC makers.

The survey underscored that Celetron's disciplined focus on capital-intensive automation coupled with high-dexterity cleanroom assembly gave it a commanding cost advantage over Southeast Asian competitors.
sourceNote: Electronics For You Annual Top 100 Survey, December 2002.

title: Hard Drives Deliver: JTS Technology Storms Top 20 with Rs 622 Cr Hardware Exports
subtitle: Dataquest Top 20 Annual Hardware Survey Chronicles How JTS Technology Vaulted into India's Elite Infotech Ranks
leadQuote: Storming the Top 20 bastion, this Tandon Group company vaulted into India's top infotech rankings on the back of ₹622.7 crore in hard drive manufacturing exports.
paragraphs: In its definitive annual Top 20 industry survey, Dataquest recorded a historic milestone for Indian electronics manufacturing: JTS Technology, an integral arm of the Tandon Group, surged into the national Top 20 rankings with an astounding ₹622.7 crore in audited export turnover.

Specializing in high-capacity 3.5-inch and 2.5-inch hard disk drive assembly and precision magneto-resistive head stacking at SEEPZ, Mumbai, JTS demonstrated that India could operate at the frontier of micro-storage technology.

The survey noted that JTS single-handedly accounted for the vast majority of hard disk drive shipments originating from the Indian subcontinent, validating Chairman M.L. Tandon's thesis that high-volume precision engineering could thrive in India's export zones.
sourceNote: Dataquest Top 20 Volume XV, Issue 13, July 15, 1997.

title: ESC Awards for Excellence in Exports: Honouring Industry Leaders
subtitle: Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council Recognizes Top National Exporters in New Delhi
leadQuote: Recognizing the enterprises that have established India's electronic hardware reputation across the global economy.
paragraphs: The February 1996 edition of Elsoftex Newsletter documented the annual Export Excellence Awards ceremony organized by the Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC).

Chaired by Mr. M. L. Tandon, the council conferred national export trophies and certificates of excellence upon the pioneers who expanded India's foreign exchange earnings across North America, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific.
The citations commended member unitholders for maintaining international zero-defect quality thresholds while navigating intense global price competition.
sourceNote: Elsoftex Newsletter, February 1996 (Awards Special Edition).

title: Message From the Chairman: Leading India Through the Electronics Revolution
subtitle: New Year Policy Vision by Shri M.L. Tandon, Chairman ESC, on Global Competitiveness and Technological Self-Reliance
leadQuote: As we stand on the threshold of a new millennium, India's destiny in the global information era will be defined by our commitment to manufacturing precision and quality excellence.
paragraphs: In his New Year message as Chairman of the Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC), Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon urged Indian industrialists and policymakers to adopt a long-term strategic vision for global trade.

Mr. Tandon warned against complacency, pointing out that while software exports were capturing public headlines, a robust domestic and export economy must be anchored by physical hardware manufacturing capabilities.

He called upon the Ministry of Commerce and state governments to streamline customs protocols, establish world-class air cargo infrastructure, and create bonded manufacturing parks to match the rapid expansion of East Asian technology zones.
sourceNote: Elsoftex Newsletter, Volume XVI, January 1996, Chairman's Editorial Column.

title: Electronics Exports — Performance & Prospects: Dialogue with M.L. Tandon
subtitle: International Technology Journal Electronic Business Asia Interviews M.L. Tandon on Operating India's Largest Cleanroom Export Infrastructure
leadQuote: Indian cleanroom operations offer extraordinary precision dexterity. When paired with international management standards, our output rivals any cleanroom in the Pacific Rim.
paragraphs: In a feature interview conducted by international tech journal Electronic Business Asia, Mr. Manohar Lal Tandon discussed the mechanics of operating tier-one hardware manufacturing units in India.

Addressing overseas investors and global electronics procurement executives, Mr. Tandon detailed the operational advantages of Mumbai's SEEPZ: duty-free capital equipment imports, direct satellite data connectivity, and an educated, English-speaking technical workforce.

He explained how the Tandon Group had maintained multi-year contracts with IBM, Compaq, and Conner Peripherals by implementing rigorous statistical process control and continuous operator certification programs.
sourceNote: Electronic Business Asia, November 25, 1995.

title: The DQ Top 20: Tandon Group Exporters — Advance Technology Devices & Tancom Electronics
subtitle: Dataquest Annual Survey Ranks Tandon Group Entities as India's Top Hardware Export Powerhouses
leadQuote: Year after year, the Tandon Group companies — Advance Technology Devices and Tancom Electronics — set the gold standard for Indian electronics exports.
paragraphs: In Dataquest's 1995 Top 20 survey, the Tandon Group's operating units at SEEPZ, Mumbai — Advance Technology Devices (ATD) and Tancom Electronics — were once again affirmed as India's foremost hardware manufacturing exporters.

The survey highlighted the group's dominance in magnetic storage heads, precision voice-coil motors, and switch-mode power supplies, which accounted for substantial foreign exchange earnings and set the pace for the domestic electronics sector.

Dataquest commended Mr. M. L. Tandon's forward-thinking investments in automated surface mount technology and cleanroom inspection systems, which allowed the group to satisfy stringent quality audits by global tech leaders.
sourceNote: Dataquest Top 20, August 1–15, 1995.

title: CT 101 Key Infotech Companies: Tandon Group Ranked Top 4 Hardware Manufacturer
subtitle: Computers Today Directory of India's 101 Premier Technology Corporations Profiles the Tandon Group's Manufacturing Scale
leadQuote: Ranking among India's top four computer hardware companies, the Tandon Group stands unmatched in export volumes and cleanroom precision manufacturing.
paragraphs: In the CT 101 Key Infotech Companies directory published by Computers Today in June 1994, the Tandon Group was ranked among the top four computer hardware enterprises in India, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with HCL-HP and Wipro Infotech.

The profile detailed the company's multi-unit manufacturing complex at SEEPZ, Mumbai, highlighting its production of floppy disk drives, Winchester heads, and certified switch-mode power supplies for global computer systems.
Under the leadership of CEO Manohar Lal Tandon, the group had expanded its workforce beyond 5,000 employees while dedicating over 95 per cent of its output to high-value foreign exports.
sourceNote: Computers Today CT 101 Directory, June 1994.
